title: Frikadeller
subtitle: Danish pork patties
excerpt: Soft pork mince patties seasoned with allspice and pan-fried in butter until golden. Frikadeller are Denmark's everyday meat patties, eaten hot with potatoes and pickled red cabbage or cold the next day in a packed lunch. One of the most frequently cooked dishes in Danish homes.
sourceNotes: Frikadeller are Denmark's everyday meat patties. Made from pork mince, they are pan-fried and served with potatoes and pickled red cabbage. They are one of the most frequently cooked dishes in Danish homes.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze cooked patties between baking paper layers. Reheat in a pan.

content.text: Frikadeller are softer and more loosely shaped than a burger patty. The mixture should feel a little wet and yielding -- not stiff. Shape with a wet spoon and hand. Do not move them in the pan until they are ready to turn -- they will release when they have a good crust.
Combine pork mince, grated onion, eggs, flour, milk, salt, pepper, and allspice in a bowl. Mix well -- the mixture should be soft and a little loose.
Heat butter in a frying pan over medium heat.
Form patties by scooping with a large spoon and shaping with a wet hand, slightly flatter than a meatball.
Fry for 5-6 minutes per side until cooked through and deep golden. Do not move them until they are ready to turn. Cook in batches if needed.

items.fix: Cook on medium, not high heat. Remove as soon as the juices run clear.

content.text: Denmark. The Danish equivalent of a burger. Found in every family fridge, often eaten cold the next day in a packed lunch. Served hot with boiled potatoes, gravy, and pickled red cabbage.
